# data


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

Before a document can be searched it has to be cut into pieces. A search
returns pieces, not whole files: a 15-page paper should come back as the
paragraph that answers the question, not as page 1. Each piece is called
a chunk, and the object that decides where to cut is a chunker.

This page holds the tools that read files and produce chunks, plus the
functions that clean up a query before it reaches SQLite’s full-text
search. Most applications never call them directly, because
[`Index.add`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index.add)
and `add_dir` in `litesearch.tree` call them for you. Reach for them
when you build your own pipeline on
[`database()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database),
or when you want to see what a file turns into before you index it.

The sections, in order: reading PDFs, chunking text, reading code and
other files, profiles for special document kinds, listing installed
packages, preparing queries, and building a PDF from images.

## Reading PDFs

[pdf_oxide](https://github.com/yfedoseev/pdf-oxide) opens and reads
PDFs. litesearch adds a few methods to its `PdfDocument` class, each
taking an optional page range `st` to `end` (0-based, `end` excluded,
all pages by default):

### PdfDocument.pdf_texts

``` python
def pdf_texts(

```

*The plain text of each page from `st` to `end`.*

[`pdf_parse`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pdf_parse)
is the function to use when you index a PDF. It returns a list with one
markdown string per page. The work is done by
[pdflite](https://github.com/vedicreader/pdflite), a separate package
whose helpers are re-exported here. pdflite converts each page with
pdf_oxide, joins words hyphenated across a line break, and collapses the
extra spaces and blank lines the conversion leaves. Some pages come out
with their columns scrambled, so that a figure such as a price ends up
on a line of its own, away from its label. For those pages pdflite tries
the plain-text layer instead and keeps whichever version strands fewer
values.

A scanned book has no text layer at all, only page images, and needs OCR
(optical character recognition, reading the text from the images).
`ocr_selection` controls it. With `'auto'`, the default, OCR runs over
the whole document when pdf_oxide reports any page as scanned. `'on'`
always runs it and `'off'` never does. OCR needs the `liteparse`
package, which is not installed with litesearch.

Images on the pages are saved to `out_path/image_dir`, and the markdown
links to them by that relative path. With no `out_path`, they go to
`pdfs/images` under the current folder. `preserve_layout=True` keeps
indentation and runs of spaces, which tables laid out with spaces need.

[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) and
`add_dir` call
[`pdf_parse`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pdf_parse)
and keep its page boundaries. The document tree and the default chunk
size were both measured on this one-string-per-page split.

``` python
def pdf_parse(
    pdf:pdf_oxide.pdf_oxide.PdfDocument | str | pathlib.Path | bytes,
    out_path:str | pathlib.Path=None, # folder that holds the image folder (default `pdfs`); image links in the markdown are relative to it
    image_dir:str='images', # name of the folder, inside `out_path`, that extracted images are saved to
    preserve_layout:bool=False, # keep indentation and runs of spaces, which space-aligned tables need
    ocr_selection:str='auto', # 'auto' runs OCR when pdf_oxide reports a scanned page; 'on' always, 'off' never
)->list:
```

*A PDF as a list of markdown strings, one per page, with OCR for scanned
documents.*

## Chunking text

The default chunker is chonkie’s `FastChunker`, set to 512 bytes. It
walks through the text and cuts each piece at the last newline, full
stop or question mark before the 512-byte limit, so a chunk usually ends
at the end of a line or sentence. Where there is none, it cuts at the
limit. 512 bytes is about 500 characters of English, or about 170
characters of Devanagari, which takes three bytes per letter. `evals/`
measured 512-byte chunks against page-sized ones, and the smaller chunks
found the right section more often.

#### `SafeFastChunker`

`FastChunker` cuts by byte position, so a cut can land in the middle of
a character that takes more than one byte, such as an em dash, a curly
quote or any Devanagari letter. It then raises `UnicodeDecodeError`, and
a long unbroken paragraph with one such character, which most scraped
web pages contain, is enough to trigger it. `SafeFastChunker` moves each
cut back to the start of the character it split. No text is lost; a cut
moves by at most three bytes. litesearch uses it everywhere in place of
`FastChunker`.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<a
href="https://github.com/Karthik777/litesearch/blob/main/litesearch/data.py#L99"

### **getattr**

``` python
def __getattr__(
    nm
):
```

``` python
from chonkie import FastChunker
SafeFastChunker = _safe_chunker()
assert SafeFastChunker is _safe_chunker() and issubclass(SafeFastChunker, FastChunker)
```

Importing litesearch does not import chonkie, model2vec, tokenizers or
codesigs. Importing chonkie alone takes about 190 ms, and a process that
only searches an existing store never needs any of them. Each is
imported the first time a function that needs it runs. The test below
checks this in a fresh Python process.

``` python
import subprocess, sys
_heavy = ['chonkie', 'chonkie_core', 'model2vec', 'tokenizers', 'codesigs']
_chk = f"""import sys, litesearch
from litesearch import correct, fts_or, fts_phrases, rank_fts, rrf_all, doc_encoder, query_encoder, static_embedder
print([m for m in {_heavy!r} if m in sys.modules])"""
assert subprocess.run([sys.executable, '-c', _chk], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout.strip() == '[]'
_chk = "import sys, litesearch; litesearch.chunk_markdown('a b'); print(litesearch.SafeFastChunker.__name__, 'chonkie' in sys.modules)"
assert subprocess.run([sys.executable, '-c', _chk], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout.strip() == 'SafeFastChunker True'
```

### chunk_markdown

``` python
def chunk_markdown(
    text:str, # markdown text (e.g. one page from pdf_parse())
    chunker:BaseChunker=None, # any chonkie chunker; None uses a 512-byte SafeFastChunker
)->fastcore.foundation.L:
```

``` python
_pdf2 = next((p for p in ['pdfs/attention_is_all_you_need.pdf', 'nbs/pdfs/attention_is_all_you_need.pdf'] if Path(p).exists()), None)
if _pdf2:
    _doc = PdfDocument(_pdf2)
    _chunks = _doc.pdf_chunks()
    assert len(_chunks) > 0
    assert all(len(t) == 3 for t in _chunks), 'each chunk must be (page, chunk_idx, text)'
    print(f'pdf_chunks: {len(_chunks)} chunks from {_doc.page_count()} pages (sample: {repr(_chunks[0][2][:60])})...')
else:
    print('Skipping chunk test — PDF not found')
```

    pdf_chunks: 98 chunks from 15 pages (sample: 'Provided proper attribution is provided, Google hereby grant')...

There are three ways to chunk text:

- `chunk_markdown(text)` returns the chunks as a list of strings. Use it
  when you only need the text.
- `chunk_spans(text)` returns `(start, end, text)` for each chunk, as
  character positions in the string you passed in. Use it when you need
  to map a chunk back to its place in the source, for example to
  highlight a hit inside the full document.
- [`PdfDocument.pdf_chunks()`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pdfdocument.pdf_chunks)
  runs
  [`pdf_parse`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pdf_parse)
  and then
  [`chunk_markdown`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#chunk_markdown)
  on each page, and returns `(page, chunk_idx, text)`. Pages are counted
  from 1 and `chunk_idx` restarts at 0 on each page. Use it to index a
  PDF page by page without building a document tree.

All three take an optional `chunker`, any chonkie chunker, if 512 bytes
does not suit your text.

### chunk_spans

``` python
def chunk_spans(
    text:str, # text to split
    chunker:BaseChunker=None, # any chonkie chunker; None uses a 512-byte SafeFastChunker
)->fastcore.foundation.L:
```

*Split text into chunks and return each as `(start, end, text)`, where
`text[start:end]` gives the chunk back.*

``` python
_t = "First sentence here. Second sentence follows. Third one ends it."
_spans = chunk_spans(_t)
assert len(_spans) >= 1
for s,e,txt in _spans:
    assert _t[s:e] == txt          # offsets index back into the original text exactly
assert _spans[0][0] == 0           # first chunk starts at 0
```

``` python
for _bad in ['a'*510 + '—' + 'b'*600,     # the cut lands mid-character
             'a'*400 + '—'*200,           # every candidate cut is mid-character
             '—'*700]:
    assert ''.join(chunk_markdown(_bad)) == _bad, 'text lost or altered by chunking'
    for s, e, txt in chunk_spans(_bad): assert _bad[s:e] == txt

# the upstream chunker on the same input is what used to reach `add_doc`
try: FastChunker(chunk_size=512)('a'*510 + '—' + 'b'*600); assert False, 'chonkie fixed it upstream'
except UnicodeDecodeError: pass

# a paragraph split still happens where it should, and ASCII text chunks exactly as before
_para = ('x'*200 + '\n\n')*3
assert chunk_markdown(_para, SafeFastChunker(chunk_size=512, delimiters='\n\n')) == \
       chunk_markdown(_para, FastChunker(chunk_size=512, delimiters='\n\n'))
```

## Reading code and other files

Code needs different chunks from prose. A 512-byte cut through the
middle of a function is useless as a search result, so code is cut at
definitions instead: each top-level function or class becomes one chunk.
Every chunk is a dict with the text under `content` and facts about
where it came from under `metadata`, which is the shape `get_store` and
`sync` in `litesearch.core` take.

`file_parse(path)` picks a reader by the file’s extension:

<th>one chunk per</th>
</tr>
</thead>

<td>top-level function or class, plus imports or assignments if
asked</td>
</tr>
<tr>

Any other extension gives an empty list. For languages other than Python
only the signatures are indexed, through the
[codesigs](https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/codesigs) package, so a search
finds the function by its name and parameters but not by what its body
does.

To read many files at once,
[`pkg2chunks`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pkg2chunks)
reads every file of an installed package and
[`dir2chunks`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#dir2chunks)
every file under a folder. Both are further down.

## Profiles: how to read one kind of document

Some documents need more than a different chunker. A Sanskrit text in
TEI XML, for example, needs a reader that knows an `<lg xml:id=...>`
element is a verse, a tree that treats a citation as the start of a
chapter, and a chunker that cuts at the daṇḍa (।), the mark that ends a
half-verse. A
[`Profile`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#profile)
bundles all of these for one kind of document and gives them a name.
When `add_file` or `add_dir` in `litesearch.tree` reads a file, it asks
[`profile_for`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#profile_for)
whether a registered profile claims it. If one does, the profile’s parts
are used; if none does, the file goes through the default pipeline
above.

#### [`Profile`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#profile)

The fields, all optional except `name`:

<table>
<colgroup>
<col style="width: 50%" />
<col style="width: 50%" />
</colgroup>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>field</th>
<th>what it is</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>exts</code></td>
<td>the extensions the profile claims, comma-separated, such as
<code>'.xml,.txt'</code>; empty claims every extension</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>detect</code></td>
<td>a function from the file’s text to True or False, used when an
extension is shared</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>parse</code></td>
<td>a function from a path to <code>(pages, meta)</code>, used instead
of the default reader</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>chunker</code></td>
<td>a function returning a chonkie chunker, used instead of the 512-byte
default</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>mode</code></td>
<td>the structure mode for <a
href="https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#build_tree"><code>build_tree</code></a>,
used instead of detecting one</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>kind</code></td>
<td>the document kind recorded on the document’s row, so searches can
filter on it</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>meta</code></td>
<td>a function from a chunk’s text to a dict, stored in the chunk’s
<code>metadata</code> column</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

`meta` lets a profile attach facts that only it can work out. ganapati’s
Sanskrit profile stores each verse’s metre there. The `metadata` column
is part of the full-text index that `get_store` builds, so those facts
become searchable and filterable with no change to the table.

#### [`profile_for`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#profile_for)

[`profile_for`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#profile_for)
returns the first registered profile that claims a file, or None. It
checks the extension first and then calls `detect` on up to the first
60,000 characters of the file. An extension alone is never enough to
decide: `.xml` may be TEI, a vedicreader export or something unrelated,
and `.txt` may be anything. A profile that has no `detect` and shares
its extension with another can still be chosen by passing `name=`.
[`register_profile`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#register_profile)
adds a profile, replacing any with the same name.

### Profile

``` python
def Profile(
    name:str, exts:str='', parse:<built-in function callable>=None, chunker:<built-in function callable>=None,
    mode:str=None, detect:<built-in function callable>=None, kind:str=None, meta:<built-in function callable>=None
)->None:
```

*How to read one kind of document: its reader, structure mode, chunker
and extra metadata.*

Another package can add profiles without litesearch importing it, and
without importing litesearch itself. It declares an entry point in the
`litesearch.profiles` group that names a function, and that function
calls
[`register_profile`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#register_profile).
The first call to
[`profile_for`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#profile_for)
runs
[`load_plugins`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#load_plugins),
which calls each such function once. A plugin that raises is skipped
with a warning, and the others still load. ganapati registers its
Sanskrit profiles this way:

``` toml
[project.entry-points."litesearch.profiles"]
ganapati = "ganapati.lemma:register_profiles"
```

``` python
from types import SimpleNamespace
from fastcore.test import test_eq
ep = SimpleNamespace(name='zz', load=lambda: lambda: register_profile(Profile('zz_test', exts='.zz')))
bad = SimpleNamespace(name='bad', load=lambda: 1/0)
import warnings
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as ws:
    warnings.simplefilter('always')
    test_eq(load_plugins([ep, bad]), ['zz'])             # a broken plugin warns, the rest still load
assert any('bad' in str(w.message) for w in ws)
test_eq(profile_for('a.zz').name, 'zz_test')
PROFILES.pop('zz_test');
```

[`ipynb_parse`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#ipynb_parse)
returns every cell of a notebook, code, markdown and raw alike. Here is
the first cell of this project’s core notebook:

``` python
ipynb_parse(Path('01_core.ipynb'))[0]
```

[`pyparse`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pyparse)
reads a Python file, or a string of code passed as `code=`, and returns
one chunk per top-level function and class. Methods stay inside their
class’s chunk, and a function defined inside another function stays
inside it. The metadata gives the name, the node type (`FunctionDef`,
`ClassDef` and so on), the first and last line, the file’s path and its
modification time. With `code=` there is no file, so `path` is the
string `'None'` and `uploaded_at` is None.

It reads only the top level of the module and splits the source into
lines once per file. On 400 files of the `transformers` package that
took parsing from 23.4 s to 3.3 s with the same chunks.

``` python
txt = """
from fastcore.all import *
a=1
class SomeClass:
    def __init__(self,x): store_attr()
    def method(self): return self.x + a
 """
pyparse(code=txt)
```

    [{'content': 'class SomeClass:\n    def __init__(self,x): store_attr()\n    def method(self): return self.x + a', 'metadata': {'path': 'None', 'uploaded_at': None, 'name': 'SomeClass', 'lang': '.py', 'type': 'ClassDef', 'lineno': 4, 'end_lineno': 6}}]

With `imports=True` it also returns each `from ... import ...`
statement. A plain `import x` statement is not included.

``` python
pyparse(code=txt, imports=True)
```

    [{'content': 'from fastcore.all import *', 'metadata': {'path': 'None', 'uploaded_at': None, 'name': None, 'lang': '.py', 'type': 'ImportFrom', 'lineno': 2, 'end_lineno': 2}}, {'content': 'class SomeClass:\n    def __init__(self,x): store_attr()\n    def method(self): return self.x + a', 'metadata': {'path': 'None', 'uploaded_at': None, 'name': 'SomeClass', 'lang': '.py', 'type': 'ClassDef', 'lineno': 4, 'end_lineno': 6}}]

``` python
pyparse(code=txt, assigns=True)
```

For a JavaScript file
[`file_parse`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#file_parse)
hands over to codesigs, which returns each function’s signature with its
body replaced by `{...}`. The top-level `const` and `let` lines are not
chunks.

``` python
def parse_js():
    from textwrap import dedent
    from tempfile import NamedTemporaryFile as ntf

    js_code = dedent("""
        const htmlElement = document.documentElement;
        const mediaQuery = window.matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)');
        const vr = '__VR__';
        let __VR__ = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(vr) || '{{__state__}}');
        function storeState(key, value) {__VR__[key] = value; localStorage.setItem(vr, JSON.stringify(__VR__));}
        function getState(key){return __VR__[key];}
        function removeState(key) {delete  __VR__[key]; localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(__VR__)); }
        function setTheme(color,fn=null, ...args) {
            if (color === null || color === undefined) {return;}
            htmlElement.classList.remove(__VR__.theme);
            htmlElement.classList.add(color);
            storeState('theme', color);
            if (typeof fn === 'function') {fn(...args);}
        }
    """)

    with ntf('w+', suffix='.js', encoding='utf-8') as f:
        f.write(js_code)
        f.flush()  # Ensure content is readable by file_parse from disk
        print(file_parse(Path(f.name)))

parse_js()
```

    [{'content': 'function storeState(key, value) {...}', 'metadata': {'path': '/tmp/tmpfpafitq6.js', 'uploaded_at': 1792653836.8016536, 'lang': '.js'}}, {'content': 'function getState(key) {...}', 'metadata': {'path': '/tmp/tmpfpafitq6.js', 'uploaded_at': 1792653836.8016536, 'lang': '.js'}}, {'content': 'function removeState(key) {...}', 'metadata': {'path': '/tmp/tmpfpafitq6.js', 'uploaded_at': 1792653836.8016536, 'lang': '.js'}}, {'content': 'function setTheme(color,fn=null, ...args) {...}', 'metadata': {'path': '/tmp/tmpfpafitq6.js', 'uploaded_at': 1792653836.8016536, 'lang': '.js'}}]

[`globsafe`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#globsafe)
takes the parameters of fastcore’s `globtastic` and returns the same
files, but skips an entry it cannot read. `globtastic` raises `OSError`
at a symlink that points at itself, and returns a dangling link as if it
were a file.
[`globsafe`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#globsafe)
leaves out both, and an unreadable folder, and does not enter a
symlinked folder that leads back into one of its own ancestors.
[`pkg2files`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pkg2files)
and
[`dir2files`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#dir2files)
use it.

``` python
def globsafe(
    path:pathlib.Path | str='.', # folder to walk
    recursive:bool=True, maxdepth:int=None, symlinks:bool=True, file_glob:str=None, file_re:str=None,
    path_glob:str=None, path_re:str=None, folder_re:str=None, skip_file_glob:str=None, skip_file_re:str=None,
    skip_folder_re:str=None, func:<built-in function callable>=walk_join, ret_folders:bool=False, sort:bool=True,
    types:str | list=None, exts:str | list=None
)->fastcore.foundation.L:
```

*`globtastic` that skips symlink loops, dangling links and unreadable
folders instead of raising.*

``` python
def pkg2files(
    pkg:str, # installed package, by import or distribution name
    skip_file_re:str='^[.]|^(?:setup\\.py|conftest\\.py)$', # regex of file names to skip
    skip_folder_re:str='^[.]|^(?:tests?|examples?|docs?|build|dist|_proc|_docs|_site|_site_libs|node_modules|__pycache__)$', # regex of folder names to skip
    func:type=Path, # applied to each path, such as Path or str
    path:list=None, # site-packages folders to look in; None looks in the running interpreter
    *, recursive:bool=True, maxdepth:int=None, symlinks:bool=True, file_glob:str=None, file_re:str=None,
    path_glob:str=None, path_re:str=None, folder_re:str=None, skip_file_glob:str=None, ret_folders:bool=False,
    sort:bool=True, types:str | list=None, exts:str | list=None
)->fastcore.foundation.L: # passed to globsafe, such as `exts=code_exts`
```

*Every file in an installed package’s folder, skipping tests, docs,
build output and hidden files.*

A folder with a file symlinked to itself, a dangling link and a link
back to its parent still lists its real files. On a tree without such
entries
[`globsafe`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#globsafe)
returns what `globtastic` does.

``` python
_lp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'loops'; (_lp/'sub').mkdir(parents=True)
for _n in ('a.py', 'sub/b.py'): (_lp/_n).write_text('x = 1\n')
(_lp/'loop.jpg').symlink_to(_lp/'loop.jpg'); (_lp/'gone.py').symlink_to(_lp/'nowhere.py'); (_lp/'sub'/'up').symlink_to(_lp)
_fc = Path(spec('fastcore').origin).parent
test_eq(globsafe(_fc, exts='py', skip_folder_re='__pycache__'), globtastic(_fc, exts='py', skip_folder_re='__pycache__'))
dir2files(_lp).map(lambda p: str(p.relative_to(_lp)))
```

With `path=` a package is looked up in those site-packages folders
instead of the running interpreter’s, and its version comes from the
`dist-info` found there. `kkfake` is installed in neither.

``` python
_sp = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())/'site-packages'; (_sp/'kkfake').mkdir(parents=True)
(_sp/'kkfake'/'__init__.py').write_text('def hello(): return 1\n')
(_sp/'kkfake-1.0.dist-info').mkdir()
(_sp/'kkfake-1.0.dist-info'/'METADATA').write_text('Metadata-Version: 2.1\nName: kkfake\nVersion: 1.0\nAuthor-email: a@b.co\n')
test_eq(spec('kkfake'), None)
test_eq(pkg_dist('kkfake', [_sp]).version, '1.0')
pkg2files('kkfake', path=[_sp]).map(lambda p: p.name)
```

### dir2chunks

``` python
def dir2chunks(
    dir:str, # directory path
    imports:bool=False, # include import statements as code chunks
    assigns:bool=False, # include top-level assignments as code chunks
    n_workers:int=None, # parse workers; 0 is serial, None picks by file count
    threadpool:bool=False, # threads rather than processes (see `_parse_files`)
    *, skip_file_re:str='^[.]|^(?:setup\\.py|conftest\\.py)$', # regex of file names to skip
    skip_folder_re:str='^[.]|^(?:tests?|examples?|docs?|build|dist|_proc|_docs|_site|_site_libs|node_modules|__pycache__)$', # regex of folder names to skip
    func:type=Path, # applied to each path, such as Path or str
    path:pathlib.Path | str='.', # folder to walk
    recursive:bool=True, maxdepth:int=None, symlinks:bool=True, file_glob:str=None, file_re:str=None,
    path_glob:str=None, path_re:str=None, folder_re:str=None, skip_file_glob:str=None, ret_folders:bool=False,
    sort:bool=True, types:str | list=None, exts:str | list=None
)->fastcore.foundation.L: # passed to dir2files, such as `exts=` or `types=`
```

*Chunks for every file under a folder, with the folder in their
metadata.*

### pkg2chunks

``` python
def pkg2chunks(
    pkg:str, # package name
    imports:bool=False, # include import statements as code chunks
    n_workers:int=None, # parse workers; 0 is serial, None picks by file count
    threadpool:bool=False, # threads rather than processes (see `_parse_files`)
    path:list=None, # site-packages folders to read the package from; None uses the running interpreter
    **kw
)->fastcore.foundation.L: # passed to pkg2files, such as `exts=code_exts`
```

*Chunks for every file of an installed package, with the package name
and version in their metadata.*

[`pkg2chunks`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pkg2chunks)
reads a whole installed package, which is how you make a library’s
source searchable.
[`dir2chunks`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#dir2chunks)
does the same for a folder, such as your own repository. Both find the
files with
[`pkg2files`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pkg2files)
or
[`dir2files`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#dir2files),
read each with
[`file_parse`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#file_parse),
and add to the metadata: the package name and version, or the folder.

The two file listers skip hidden files and folders, `setup.py`,
`conftest.py`, and folders named `test`, `tests`, `example`, `examples`,
`doc`, `docs`, `build`, `dist`, `node_modules`, `__pycache__`, and
nbdev’s generated `_proc`,
[`_docs`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#_docs),
`_site` and `_site_libs`. They return every other file, so pass
`exts=code_exts` (or a list of extensions) to keep to code.

From 64 files up, the files are read in a pool of processes, one per
CPU. Processes are used rather than threads because parsing holds
Python’s global interpreter lock the whole time: over 2,170 files, four
threads ran at 0.76 times the speed of one, and four processes at 3.37
times. Pass `n_workers=0` to read in the current process.

``` python
pkg2chunks('fastlite').filter(lambda d: d['metadata']['type']=='FunctionDef')[0]
```

### installed_packages

``` python
def installed_packages(
    nms:list=None, # package names or requirement strings; None lists every installed package
    pyproject:bool=False, # also include the dependencies in the current repository's pyproject.toml
    xtras:str | None=None, # comma-separated `[dependency-groups]` from pyproject.toml to include too
    path:list=None, # site-packages folders to look in; None looks in the running interpreter
)->fastcore.foundation.L:
```

*The names of installed packages, all of them or only those asked for,
leaving out the standard library.*

[`installed_packages`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#installed_packages)
tells you which packages in an environment you could index with
[`pkg2chunks`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pkg2chunks).
Called with a list of names, it returns those that are installed and
drops the rest. With `pyproject=True` it adds the dependencies listed in
the current repository’s `pyproject.toml`, and `xtras` adds named
dependency groups from the same file. With no arguments it lists every
installed distribution.

The standard library is left out by checking each distribution’s
`Author-email` metadata, so a package that does not set that field is
left out too. In the first example below, `fstlite` is a misspelling
that is not installed, so only the `pyproject.toml` dependencies come
back.

``` python
installed_packages(['fstlite'], pyproject=True, xtras='foo') # non existent package
```

    ['pdflite', 'chonkie', 'pillow', 'model2vec', 'tokenizers', 'pdf_oxide', 'fastlite', 'usearch', 'codesigs']

``` python
installed_packages(['fastlite']) # existing package
```

    ['fastlite']

``` python
installed_packages('rishi[all]')
```

    ['rishi']

`path=` narrows
[`installed_packages`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#installed_packages)
the same way: the `kkfake` package from the
[`pkg2files`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pkg2files)
example above is the only one listed.

``` python
test_eq(installed_packages(['kkfake'], path=[_sp]), ['kkfake'])
installed_packages(path=[_sp])
```

``` python
_ls = spec('litesearch')
assert _ls and spec('litesearch[sanskrit]')
assert spec('litesearch[sanskrit]').name == _ls.name
assert 'litesearch' in installed_packages(['litesearch[sanskrit]'])

_rishi = spec('rishi')
if _rishi:
    assert spec('rishi[all]')
    assert spec('rishi[all]').name == _rishi.name
    assert 'rishi' in installed_packages(['rishi[all]'])
```

``` python
installed_packages()[:10] # all installed packages that are not stdlib
```

## Preparing a query for full-text search

SQLite’s full-text search engine, FTS5, finds rows that contain the
words of a query and ranks them with bm25, a score that rewards rare
words and words that appear often in a short row. Its query language
gives several characters a special meaning: `*` marks a prefix, `"`
quotes a phrase, parentheses group terms, `^` anchors a term to the
start of a column, `-` belongs to the syntax for choosing columns, and
`OR`, `AND` and `NOT` combine terms. A word may contain only letters,
digits and `_` unless it is quoted. A question typed by a user can
therefore fail with a syntax error, and even a valid one asks for too
much: by default FTS5 returns only rows that contain every word,
including words such as “how” and “does”.

These functions turn a user’s text into a query FTS5 accepts and that
finds more:

- [`clean`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#clean)
  replaces the operator characters `* , " ( ) ^`, and a `-` directly
  before a word, with spaces. It returns None for an empty query.
  Underscores are kept, so `fts_search` stays one word.
- [`kw`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#kw) splits
  the text into words with the Unicode word-boundary rules (UAX \#29,
  through apsw), lowercases them, and drops one-letter words and the
  stopwords in `QSTOP`, a list of common English words such as “the”,
  “how” and “does”. If every word is a stopword, it keeps them all.
- [`add_wc`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#add_wc)
  adds `*` to each word so it also matches longer words that start with
  it: `sample*` matches “samples”. A word with characters other than
  ASCII letters, digits and `_`, such as `pathfinder's` or any
  Devanagari word, is quoted first, because FTS5 accepts it only as a
  quoted string.
- [`mk_wider`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#mk_wider)
  joins the words with `OR`, so a row needs only one of them to match.
  bm25 still ranks rows that match more of the words higher.
- [`pre`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pre) runs
  all four in that order:
  [`clean`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#clean),
  [`kw`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#kw),
  [`add_wc`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#add_wc),
  [`mk_wider`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#mk_wider).
  Each step after
  [`clean`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#clean) can
  be turned off.

[`Database.search`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#database.search)
passes the keyword half of every search through
[`pre`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#pre) unless
you set `fts_pre=False`. `evals/` measured it at +0.016 to +0.093
weighted MRR. To build a query from a list of terms you already have,
rather than from a user’s sentence, use
[`fts_or`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#fts_or),
[`fts_and`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#fts_and)
or
[`fts_phrases`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/core.html#fts_phrases)
in `litesearch.core`, which quote each term.

### clean

``` python
def clean(
    q:str, # the user's query
    pattern:str='[*,"\\(\\)\\^]|-(?=\\S)', # characters to replace with a space
):
```

*Replace FTS5 operator characters in `q` with spaces; None when nothing
is left.*

The default output for “This is a sample query” is `sample* OR query*`:
“this”, “is” and “a” are stopwords, and the two words left become
prefixes joined by `OR`. Each later line turns off steps to show the
others alone.

``` python
q = 'This is a sample query'
print('preprocessed q with defaults: `%s`' %pre(q))
print('keywords extracted: `%s`' %pre(q, wc=False, wide=False))
print('q with wild card: `%s`' %pre(q, extract_kw=False, wide=False, wc=True))
print('remove _ : `%s`' %pre('This_is_a_query_with_underscores with_uv', extract_kw=False))
```

    preprocessed q with defaults: `sample* OR query*`
    keywords extracted: `sample query`
    q with wild card: `This* is* a* sample* query*`
    remove _ : `This_is_a_query_with_underscores* OR with_uv*`

``` python
# A possessive used to make `pre` emit invalid FTS5, so `search` raised instead of searching.
# `pathfinder's*` is a syntax error; `"pathfinder's"*` is a prefix query on a string.
assert pre("The Pathfinder's transition") == '"pathfinder\'s"* OR transition*'

import apsw
_c = apsw.Connection(':memory:')
_c.execute("create virtual table t using fts5(content)")
_c.execute("insert into t values(?)", ("The Pathfinder's transition activities",))
_c.execute("insert into t values(?)", ('something else entirely',))
_q = pre("Pathfinder's activities")
assert len(list(_c.execute("select content from t where t match ?", (_q,)))) == 1
```

``` python
# a query of operator characters alone used to raise AttributeError
for q in ('***', '""', '---', '(^)', '   '): assert pre(q) is None, q
```

## Building a PDF from images

Photos or scans of pages often arrive as image files.
[`images_to_pdf`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#images_to_pdf)
puts a list of images into one PDF, one image per page, so they can go
through the same PDF pipeline as any other document, OCR included. It
accepts Pillow images, image bytes or file paths, and writes the PDF
itself from the PNG data, needing only Pillow and the standard library.
[`img2png`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#img2png)
converts one image to RGB PNG bytes, and
[`png_det`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/data.html#png_det)
reads a PNG’s width, height and compressed pixel data, which a PDF can
embed unchanged.

The functions were written when pdf_oxide’s `Pdf.from_image` methods
produced an empty 1.3 KB file. With pdf_oxide 0.3.77,
`Pdf.from_image_bytes` returns a full-size file, so either route now
works.

``` python
import tempfile, os
```

``` python
# find PDF relative to nbs/ (normal Jupyter) or project root (nbdev_test)
_pdf = next((p for p in ['pdfs/attention_is_all_you_need.pdf', 'nbs/pdfs/attention_is_all_you_need.pdf'] if Path(p).exists()), None)
assert _pdf, 'attention_is_all_you_need.pdf not found'

arxiv = PdfDocument(_pdf)

# pdf_texts and pdf_markdown
md_pages = arxiv.pdf_markdown()
assert len(md_pages) == arxiv.page_count(), f'Expected {arxiv.page_count()} pages, got {len(md_pages)}'
assert any('attention' in p.lower() for p in md_pages)

txt_pages = arxiv.pdf_texts()
assert len(txt_pages) == arxiv.page_count()
assert any('attention' in t.lower() for t in txt_pages)

links = arxiv.pdf_links()
assert isinstance(links, L)
print(f'pdf_texts: {len(txt_pages)} pages, pdf_markdown: {len(md_pages)} pages, pdf_links: {len(links)} links')

# images_to_pdf: build synthetic scanned PDF from a real page image
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    arxiv.to_markdown(2, include_images=True, embed_images=False, image_output_dir=tmp)
    img_bytes = open(os.path.join(tmp, os.listdir(tmp)[0]), 'rb').read()

_scanned = Path(_pdf).parent/'scanned_test.pdf'
images_to_pdf([img_bytes], output=str(_scanned))
scanned = PdfDocument(str(_scanned))
assert scanned.extract_text(0).strip() == '', 'scanned PDF should have no native text'
assert _scanned.stat().st_size > 100_000, 'scanned PDF should contain the embedded image'
print('images_to_pdf test passed:', _scanned)
```

### mv_skill_md

``` python
def mv_skill_md(
    dry_run:bool=True, dir:NoneType=None
)->None:
```

*Copy the bundled SKILL.md into the .agents, .claude and .Codex skill
folders, or with `dry_run` only print where.*

``` python
import io, tempfile, contextlib
from litesearch import data as _data
```

``` python
# dry_run used to print "Installed" too; the module's copy is used because it finds SKILL.md beside its own file
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(io.StringIO()) as o: _data.mv_skill_md(dry_run=True, dir=tmp)
    assert o.getvalue().startswith('Would copy') and 'Installed' not in o.getvalue(), o.getvalue()
    assert not list(Path(tmp).rglob('SKILL.md'))
    _data.mv_skill_md(dry_run=False, dir=tmp)
    for d in ['.agents', '.claude', '.Codex']: assert 'litesearch' in (Path(tmp)/d/'skills/litesearch/SKILL.md').read_text()
```
